P1.evidence: Setter acknowledged but notes not read back: 'I know you spoke with Kyla. Um, she gave me like a bit of a background, so I've kind of got a head start.' Same standing three-part frame — where you're at, what you want, alignment then coaching — missing what's in the way and what you need. Agreement asked and given, if thinly ('All right.' / 'Cool.'). Open question delivered verbatim. Worth noting that reading the setter notes back properly would have mattered more here than on any other call in the batch: the application was incomplete, and a rep who had actually reviewed it would have known that before dialling.

P2.evidence: The training-week check is the best-executed single check in the batch. 'How long do you train for now?' was asked, lost to a connection freeze, and asked again — 'Yeah, how long do you train for now?' — producing an exceptionally detailed picture covering daily circuits, tempo work, cycling, running, walking and rucking. Sleep was also asked directly, though after the disqualification: 'Sorry, did you struggle waking up or going to sleep? Or both?' Everything else was skipped. No age, height or weight. No health conditions asked, even though the prospect volunteered a year of burnout, a kratom dependency and a supervised elimination diet — a health history richer than anyone else's in this folder, none of which was probed. No injuries, no diet question, no energy question, no results from current training.

P3.evidence: No goals work. The six-month outcome question was never asked, and the prospect's stated want — variety, efficiency, effectiveness, an overhaul — was taken at face value and never developed. The one adjacent move was 'what I guess I'm curious about the most is, why do you feel like you need some coaching?', which functions as a partial bridge but was asked as a qualification challenge rather than to open motivation. Scored as reachable and missed: the disqualification came at 00:07:37 and this material was available for the seven minutes before it.

P4.evidence: No past-attempts work despite an unusually rich history freely offered — repeated burnout cycles, a substance dependency he tried and failed to moderate several times ('I'll do better this time, I won't do it as much, you know, so'), and a year on a structured elimination protocol. That is a prospect describing, in detail, a pattern of knowing what to do and not being able to hold to it, which is the exact thesis of phase 4, and none of it was picked up. 'Why do you feel like you need some coaching?' is a partial P4d at best, since its purpose was to test fit rather than to surface a structural gap.

P5.evidence: Unreachable. The rep disqualified at 00:07:37 and the prospect confirmed he had never intended to apply. Running a consequence frame on a lead you have just told you probably cannot help would be incoherent, and the phase drops out of the denominator.

P6.evidence: Unreachable for the same reason. No offer was presented, so there was nothing to obtain commitment for. The rep deliberately inverted the phase — instead of seeking a yes before presenting, he named the price and the ICP and invited the prospect to opt out.

P11.evidence: No close attempted. Nothing to collect, book, sign or send.

objection_plays.detail: The prospect's opening position was doubt about the product claim itself, and in substance it was an insinuation that the founder's physique is not achievable on the advertised training volume: 'the dude is pretty ripped, his chest is huge... I've never seen anybody that only spends 20 to 30 minutes in the gym, or whatever, looking like that.' The rep asked one good probe, 'What's got you skeptical?', and then declined the ground entirely — 'Interesting. I'm not saying it's not' — and changed the subject. None of the OE moves ran. More importantly, no evidence ran either: no client results, no explanation of intensity versus duration, no before-and-afters. This is the second call in the batch where a prospect asked for proof and was given none, and the first where the doubt went to the founder's credibility.

A prospect already well served by a free, self-directed alternative — the second known gap in the script, in its purest form. There is no scripted play for it, and the rep's improvised answer was the right one: he assessed fit honestly and disqualified. 'It sounds like you kind of, you've got a lot of things in place, nutrition-wise, sleep-wise, you're training, you know?... It doesn't really sound like we can do too much for you', followed by naming the ICP and the price and 'I'm not going to sit here and push it onto you.' Recorded as a hit and as the positive counterexample the script gap needs: on the Peter Louis call earlier the same day the same objection was answered by shrinking the offer four times. The difference between the two responses is the difference between a qualification judgement and a discount reflex, and only one of them is coachable at scale as written.

notes: A twelve-minute call that was largely correct in its conclusion and thin in its execution. The training-week question was outstanding and the disqualification was honest, transparent and made without being asked — that should be recognised, not buried. But the phases that were reachable in the first seven minutes were not run, and the prospect handed over the two things that would have changed the outcome: an explicit request for variety and better effectiveness, which the programme is well positioned to sell against, and a credibility doubt about the founder that was never answered. Coach the sequence rather than the verdict: probe fit after establishing the goal, not instead of it, because on this call the disqualification landed before anyone had established whether the prospect wanted anything at all. Also worth escalating rather than coaching — the lead should not have existed, and the rep spent twelve minutes discovering that.
